code.title: Event loop order: sync, microtasks, then tasks

followUps:
It waits in the timer machinery of the host, not on the call stack: the browser or Node keeps the timer, and only when it expires is the callback moved into the task queue. The JavaScript thread is not counting anything.

Example: setTimeout(f, 100) registers the timer and returns at once. After about 100 ms, f is queued, and it runs when the stack is empty, so the real delay can be 100 ms or more.

Run-to-completion means that once a function starts, it keeps the thread until it returns; nothing else, such as a timer, click or render, can interrupt it.

Example: if a click handler takes 200 ms, a timer due at 50 ms waits until the handler finishes. This makes shared variables safe inside one function, but long functions block everything.

Because JavaScript has one thread and the page needs that same thread to run events and paint, a long loop leaves no moment for the loop to handle clicks or draw frames.

Example: a loop that takes 3 seconds means about 180 skipped frames at 60 Hz, and clicks only register after it ends. Fix it by chunking work, using a worker, or yielding between slices.

code.title: Microtasks drain fully before the next task

followUps:
Yes: a microtask that keeps queueing another microtask means the queue never empties, so the loop never reaches the next task or paint.

Show it with a counter:

setTimeout(() => console.log('timer'), 0);
let n = 0;
function spin() { if (++n < 1e6) queueMicrotask(spin); }
spin(); // timer prints only after 1e6 microtasks

With no limit the timer never runs.

requestAnimationFrame callbacks run in the render step, after the microtasks of the current task and just before the paint, so they are neither tasks nor microtasks.

With a 60 Hz display that step comes about every 16.7 ms. A rAF callback is the right place to read layout and write DOM changes once per frame, and it pauses in background tabs.

code.title: The async1/async2 output puzzle

followUps:
It changes nothing visible in modern engines for the plain case, because an already-resolved native promise returned from an async function is treated as a value, but the details follow the promise-resolve rules.

Awaiting async2() awaits the promise that the async function itself returns, so the continuation still takes one tick: async1 end still comes before promise2. Returning a promise from .then would add extra ticks, but inside an async function the await sees one native promise.

If async2 has its own await, its promise is not fulfilled yet when async1 awaits it, so async1 end moves later.

Say async2 does await null. Then async2's remainder is queued first, and its promise resolves in a later microtask. async1's continuation is only queued once that promise resolves, so promise1 and promise2 may print before async1 end. Count the microtask queue after each job to be sure.

code.title: A generator-based async/await driver

followUps:
Write a function that steps through a generator and, for each yielded value, waits on a promise and resumes the generator with the result.

function run(g) {
  const it = g();
  return new Promise((res, rej) => {
    const step = (m, v) => { let r; try { r = it[m](v); } catch (e) { return rej(e); }
      if (r.done) return res(r.value);
      Promise.resolve(r.value).then(x => step('next', x), e => step('throw', e)); };
    step('next');
  });
}

Rejections are thrown back into the generator, so try/catch works.

A paused async function lives on the heap as a small object, not on the call stack: the engine saves its local variables and position, then pops the frame.

So 10,000 pending awaits cost 10,000 small heap objects, not 10,000 stack frames, and no stack overflow occurs. When the promise settles, the engine restores the saved state and continues on a fresh stack.

code.title: setTimeout vs then vs queueMicrotask order

followUps:
It moves promise2 before async1 end: returning a promise from an async function makes the order slower by about two ticks.

With return Promise.resolve() in async2, its own promise must adopt the returned one, which takes extra microtasks, so async1's continuation is queued late. The queue then holds promise2 first: promise1, script end, promise2, async1 end. Without the explicit return, async1 end comes first.

If async2 has its own await, its promise is not fulfilled yet when async1 awaits it, so async1 end moves later and promise2 prints first.

Say async2 does await null. After script end the microtask queue is [async2 resume, promise2]. async2 resumes and resolves its promise, and only then is async1's continuation queued, behind promise2. Count the queue after each job to be sure.

code.title: try/catch misses timer errors; three fixes

followUps:
Since Node 15, an unhandled promise rejection throws like an uncaught exception, so the process exits with a non-zero code unless a handler is registered.

Before that, Node 14 and older only printed a warning. Register process.on('unhandledRejection', fn) for logging, but treat it as a bug report: add a .catch or try/catch where the promise is created. Example: Promise.reject(new Error('x')) with no handler now crashes the script.

Pass the original error as the cause option when you throw a new one, so both messages and stack traces stay available.

try { await load(); }
catch (e) {
  throw new Error('Could not load profile', { cause: e });
}

Callers read err.cause to see the underlying error, such as a network failure. This is better than just concatenating messages, which loses the original stack.

code.title: return vs return await in try/catch/finally

followUps:
Without await, return promise leaves the try block at once, so finally runs before the promise settles and a later rejection skips the local catch.

In the program, noAwait prints its finally line first, and the caller gets the error instead of the local catch. Adding await keeps the function inside the try until the promise settles, so finally runs afterwards. Cleanup such as closing a connection is a typical case where this bug hurts.

Roughly return await p costs 1 tick for the await when p is a native promise, while return p costs about 3 ticks in total for the caller, since the async function's own promise must adopt p.

These numbers are tiny: in practice you notice them only in ordering puzzles. Choose by semantics, and use return await inside try/catch because correctness matters more than 2 microtasks.

code.title: Node ordering: nextTick, promise, immediate, timeout

followUps:
Because nextTick callbacks run right after the current operation and before the loop moves on, a nextTick that schedules another nextTick keeps the nextTick queue non-empty forever, and the loop never reaches the poll phase where I/O callbacks run.

Example: function f(){ process.nextTick(f); } f(); hangs while sockets and timers wait. Use setImmediate for recursion, because it lets I/O run between iterations.

Use setImmediate when you want to run after the current poll phase and I/O, and you want a consistent order; setTimeout(0) is subject to timer minimums and process load.

Inside an I/O callback, setImmediate always runs before any timer, which makes it predictable. It is also the right tool for splitting long work into slices because each slice lets pending I/O run.

code.title: Run-to-completion: busy loop blocks a timer

followUps:
No, an await is not completion of the whole task: the function pauses and lets other callbacks run, so anything shared can change across an await.

Example: if (balance >= 10) { await save(); balance -= 10; } is wrong because another call may spend the balance while save is pending. Re-check the state after the await, or do the update before it, or serialize calls with a queue.

Use the Long Animation Frames API (and the older Long Tasks API) through a PerformanceObserver, and report the results to your monitoring.

new PerformanceObserver(list => {
  for (const e of list.getEntries()) report(e.duration, e.scripts);
}).observe({ type: 'long-animation-frame', buffered: true });

A frame longer than 50 ms is considered long; the entries name the scripts involved, so you can see which function blocked the thread.

code.title: Microtask starvation and chunked yielding

followUps:
Because Node's nextTick queue runs to exhaustion after each operation, recursion keeps it from ever being empty, so I/O callbacks and timers are starved, and the docs warn about this.

The warning also exists because the code looks asynchronous yet is not fair. Prefer setImmediate for recursive work: each call goes to the check phase, and I/O gets a turn between iterations.

React splits rendering into small units of work and checks whether it should yield, handing control back to the browser about every 5 ms so input can run.

Its scheduler uses a MessageChannel task (not a microtask) to continue after yielding, and gives high priority to user input. So a render of 1,000 components can be paused after 5 ms, a click handled, and the render resumed, instead of one 200 ms block.

code.title: Steps of await fetch with a fake fetch

followUps:
Call abort() on an AbortController and pass its signal to fetch; the request stops and the awaiting code receives an AbortError.

const ac = new AbortController();
setTimeout(() => ac.abort(), 2000);
try { await fetch(url, { signal: ac.signal }); }
catch (e) { if (e.name !== 'AbortError') throw e; }

This also gives a timeout after 2 seconds. Ignoring the result without aborting still wastes the network.

Start all three requests first and await them together with Promise.all, rather than awaiting one after another.

const [a, b, c] = await Promise.all([get(1), get(2), get(3)]);

If each takes 100 ms, sequential awaits take about 300 ms, while Promise.all takes about 100 ms. Use Promise.allSettled if one failure must not discard the other results.

code.title: rAF vs setTimeout on a virtual clock

followUps:
Use a rAF callback to wait for the frame, then a task inside it so the code runs after the paint: requestAnimationFrame(() => setTimeout(fn)).

The rAF callback runs just before the paint, so work in it still delays the frame. The timer or MessageChannel message queued inside it becomes a task that runs after that frame has been painted. This is used to measure first paint or to start non-urgent work.

In a background tab the browser pauses rAF callbacks completely, so they never run until the tab is visible again; timers are throttled, often to once per second or less.

So do not use rAF for logic that must continue, such as polling or a game clock. Use timers, workers or the server for that, and use rAF only for drawing.

code.title: Concurrency-limited runner with shared index

followUps:
Add a shared AbortController and pass its signal to every task, then call abort() in the first failure handler.

const ac = new AbortController();
const run = t => t(ac.signal).catch(e => { ac.abort(); throw e; });
await Promise.all(tasks.map(run));

Each task must honour the signal, for example by passing it to fetch. Also set a flag so that workers stop picking up new tasks from the queue.

Races can still happen when state changes across an await, because other workers run while one is paused.

Example: two workers each do const n = count; await save(); count = n + 1;. Both read 0, and the final count is 1, not 2. The fix is to update shared state in the same synchronous step as the read, with no await in between, or to serialize the section with a queue.

code.title: Ticks: modern await vs legacy-style await

followUps:
Write the explanation as a count of microtask ticks and run it in the target runtime; the answer was different in old versions.

Example of the oldest change: in Node 10 and older, await on a native promise took 3 ticks, which is why promise2 printed first. Other changes include microtask draining between timers in Node 11, and the V8 7.2 await optimization in Node 12. Always name the version when you quote an order.

Write a test that records the order of events in an array and compares it with the expected array, and run it in CI on every supported Node and browser version.

const log = [];
queueMicrotask(() => log.push('micro'));
setTimeout(() => { log.push('task');
  assert.deepEqual(log, ['sync','micro','task']); }, 0);
log.push('sync');

Keep tests for documented guarantees (microtasks before tasks), not for exact tick counts that engines may change.
